speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** Can I deduct my home office if I work remotely?

**Jordan:** Assuming U.S. federal taxes, it depends on whether you’re an employee or self-employed. If you’re a W-2 employee, you generally can’t deduct home-office expenses on your federal return, even if your employer requires you to work from home. State rules may differ, and it’s worth asking your employer about reimbursement.

**Maya:** What if I’m self-employed?

**Jordan:** You generally qualify if you use a defined part of your home regularly and exclusively for business, and it’s your principal place of business or meets another qualifying test. A spare bedroom used only for work may qualify; a kitchen table you also use for meals generally won’t. There are exceptions to the exclusive-use rule for qualifying daycare and certain inventory storage.

**Maya:** How do I calculate the deduction?

**Jordan:** You can generally choose between two methods:

- **Simplified:** $5 per square foot of qualifying space, up to 300 square feet, for a maximum of $1,500, subject to a business-income limit.
- **Actual expenses:** Deduct eligible costs specific to the office and a business share of common costs such as rent, utilities, and insurance. Homeowners may also claim depreciation, which can have tax consequences when they sell.

**Maya:** So the simplified method means less paperwork, but it doesn’t always give me the bigger deduction?

**Jordan:** Exactly. If you qualify, compare both methods and keep records of the space, how you use it, and any expenses you claim.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** What if I have a W-2 job and also do freelance work from home?

**Jordan:** Having a W-2 job doesn’t prevent you from claiming a home-office deduction for a qualifying freelance business. But you can’t deduct expenses for your employee work. If you use the same space for both, don’t assume you can deduct a percentage based on your freelance hours—the space still has to meet the home-office qualification rules.

**Maya:** What if my freelance business barely turns a profit this year?

**Jordan:** The business-income limit can reduce or eliminate your deduction under either method. With the actual-expense method, you can generally carry forward eligible expenses that the limit prevented you from deducting. With the simplified method, you can’t carry forward the unused deduction. So if you’re comparing methods, look at more than just this year’s write-off.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** So if I use the same desk for my W-2 job during the day and freelance work at night, can I deduct half the cost?

**Jordan:** Not just by splitting the hours. A shared space generally must qualify for each business use, including meeting the convenience-of-the-employer test for your W-2 work. If you work from home at your own convenience, that use can disqualify the shared space for the freelance deduction. One option is to set aside a clearly identifiable area that you use regularly and only for qualifying freelance work. It doesn’t have to be a separate room.

**Maya:** And if the income limit wipes out my home-office deduction, do I lose my other freelance deductions?

**Jordan:** No. The home-office limit doesn’t by itself prevent you from deducting otherwise allowable business expenses, such as freelance software or supplies. Also, if you have unused actual-method home-office expenses from a prior year, choosing the simplified method this year doesn’t erase them. You can generally use them in a later year when you return to the actual-expense method, subject to that year’s income limit.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** What if I set aside a corner of my living room for freelancing, but I do most of my client work at their offices?

**Jordan:** That corner can still qualify as your principal place of business if you use it regularly and exclusively for freelance work, do administrative or management tasks there—like invoicing and scheduling—and have no other fixed location where you do substantial administrative or management work for that business. You don’t need a wall or partition, but the area must be clearly identifiable and not used for personal activities or your W-2 job.

**Maya:** And where do I claim it?

**Jordan:** If you’re a sole proprietor filing Schedule C, you generally use Form 8829 for the actual-expense method. If you choose the simplified method, calculate the deduction using the worksheet in the Schedule C instructions and report it directly on Schedule C.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** What records should I keep for that living-room corner?

**Jordan:** Keep a sketch or measurements showing the square footage you use exclusively for freelancing, plus records that show you use it regularly for business. If you use the actual-expense method, keep bills and receipts and document how you calculated the business share of costs like rent and utilities. With the simplified method, you don’t need to track those costs for the home-office deduction, but you still need to establish that the space qualifies.

**Maya:** Can I still deduct my freelance software if I use the simplified method?

**Jordan:** Yes. The simplified method replaces the calculation for expenses related to using your home, not your other business deductions. You can still deduct otherwise allowable freelance expenses, such as software and supplies, separately on Schedule C.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** What if I don’t set up the freelance corner until July?

**Jordan:** You can still qualify for the part of the year you use it regularly and exclusively for freelancing. With the simplified method, you average the qualifying square footage over all 12 months, counting a month only if you had at least 15 days of qualifying use. For example, if a 120-square-foot corner qualifies from July 1 through December 31, your average is 60 square feet. At $5 per square foot, that’s a $300 deduction before the business-income limit.

**Maya:** So I should write down when I started using it?

**Jordan:** Yes. Keep the start date with your measurements, and note any changes in the size or use of the space during the year.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** What if I use the actual-expense method instead? Can I count rent from before July?

**Jordan:** No. If the corner first qualifies in July, you generally apply the business-use percentage to eligible shared expenses, like rent and utilities, for the qualifying period only. The simplified method’s 15-day rule doesn’t apply to the actual-expense method.

**Maya:** So if the corner is 10% of my apartment and I start using it on July 1?

**Jordan:** You’d generally count 10% of your July–December rent and eligible utilities in the calculation, subject to the business-income limit. Keep the bills for that period along with your measurements and start date.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** What if I pay to repaint just the freelance corner in August?

**Jordan:** If the painting is an ordinary repair and benefits only the qualifying office area, it’s generally a direct expense. Under the actual-expense method, you’d include the full cost in the calculation, rather than just 10%, subject to the business-income limit. If you repaint the entire living room, you’d generally allocate the cost between the office and personal areas.

**Maya:** And if I buy a desk for freelancing?

**Jordan:** The desk is business furniture, not a cost of using your home. If you use it only for freelancing, you can generally deduct or depreciate it under the applicable rules, whether you choose the actual-expense or simplified method for the home office.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** What if I also use the desk for my W-2 job?

**Jordan:** There are two separate questions. For the desk itself, generally only the portion attributable to freelance use is eligible for a business deduction, subject to the rules for expensing or depreciating furniture. Keep a record of how you calculated that share.

**Maya:** Does that same percentage apply to the corner?

**Jordan:** No. The home-office deduction has its own qualification rules. Using the corner for your W-2 job can disqualify it, and tracking your freelance hours doesn’t fix that. If you want to keep the distinction clear, use the freelance corner only for freelancing and do your W-2 work elsewhere.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** So even if I can’t deduct the corner, I might still be able to deduct part of the desk?

**Jordan:** Yes. Suppose the desk cost $600 and a log from a typical workweek supports 60% freelance use. Your freelance share would be $360. That’s the amount you’d use to figure any deduction or depreciation—not necessarily what you deduct this year. Keep the receipt and a note showing how you calculated the 60%. That percentage applies to the desk, not to your rent or utilities.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** Could I deduct the whole $360 this year?

**Jordan:** Possibly. If you bought the desk and put it into use this year, the IRS’s *de minimis* safe harbor may let you deduct the $360 freelance share this year rather than depreciate it. For most sole proprietors, the limit is $2,500 per item or invoice. You must also have had a consistent practice of expensing purchases like this at the start of the year, treated the desk as an expense in your records, and attach the election to your timely filed federal return.

**Maya:** And if I don’t qualify for that election?

**Jordan:** You can generally recover the freelance share through depreciation. Either way, the desk is a separate expense: you don’t need to qualify for the home-office deduction to claim it.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** If I depreciate the desk, do I have to spread the $360 over several years?

**Jordan:** Not necessarily. If you don’t qualify for the *de minimis* safe harbor, you may still be able to deduct the full $360 in the year you put the desk into service through bonus depreciation or a Section 179 election. Bonus depreciation depends in part on when you bought the desk and started using it. Section 179 generally requires more than 50% qualifying business use and is subject to a taxable-income limit. If neither applies, office furniture is generally depreciated over seven years.

**Maya:** What if I start using the desk mostly for personal stuff next year?

**Jordan:** Keep tracking how you use it. If you claimed Section 179 and qualifying business use later drops to 50% or less during the recovery period, you generally have to report part of the earlier deduction as income. That’s a separate issue from whether your living-room corner qualifies as a home office.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** Does switching to mostly personal use also undo bonus depreciation?

**Jordan:** Generally not for an ordinary desk. The rule that can claw back a Section 179 deduction when business use drops to 50% or less doesn’t generally apply to bonus depreciation on office furniture. But if you’ve already deducted the entire $360 freelance share, there’s nothing left to depreciate. And if you stop using the desk for freelancing altogether, you can’t claim any further depreciation.

**Maya:** What if I sell it later?

**Jordan:** A sale is different from a switch to personal use. If you sell the desk at a gain, some or all of the gain on the business portion may be taxed as ordinary income under the depreciation recapture rules. Keep your purchase receipt and depreciation records even after you stop using the desk for freelancing.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** How could I have a taxable gain if I sell the desk for less than the $600 I paid?

**Jordan:** Because gain on the freelance portion is measured against its **adjusted tax basis**, not the original purchase price. Suppose you deducted the full $360 freelance share through bonus depreciation and later sold the desk for $200 while it was still 60% freelance and 40% personal. The freelance share of the sale proceeds would be $120. With a $0 basis on that share, you’d generally report the $120 as ordinary income from depreciation recapture.

**Maya:** Can I use the loss on the personal share to offset that gain?

**Jordan:** No. The personal share would have $80 in proceeds and a $240 basis, but that $160 personal loss generally isn’t deductible. You’d generally report the business portion of the sale on Form 4797.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** What if I sell the desk for less than what’s left of its business basis?

**Jordan:** Then you can generally deduct the loss on the freelance portion. Say its adjusted business basis is $250 and $120 of the sale proceeds is allocated to freelance use. You’d generally report a $130 business loss on Form 4797. Any loss on the personal portion is still nondeductible.

**Maya:** What if I never claimed depreciation?

**Jordan:** You generally still have to reduce the desk’s business basis by the depreciation you were entitled to claim, even if you didn’t claim it. That’s the “allowed or allowable” rule. If you missed deductions, check how to correct them rather than using the original $360 business basis to calculate the sale.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** How do I fix depreciation I forgot to claim?

**Jordan:** If you missed depreciation on just one filed return, you can generally amend that return if it’s still within the filing deadline for amendments. If you used the same incorrect depreciation treatment on two or more consecutively filed returns, you generally need to file Form 3115 to change your accounting method. That can let you catch up on missed depreciation through a Section 481(a) adjustment rather than amending each year.

**Maya:** What if I’ve already sold the desk?

**Jordan:** A correction may still be possible, but the timing matters. Don’t use the original $360 freelance cost as your basis just because you skipped depreciation. Before filing Form 4797, check which correction procedure applies and how much depreciation was allowable.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** Can Form 3115 still help if I sold the desk this year?

**Jordan:** Potentially. There’s a special automatic accounting-method change for certain depreciable property you dispose of. If you qualify, you generally attach Form 3115 to your timely filed original federal return, including extensions, for the year of sale. The Section 481(a) adjustment can let you catch up on missed depreciation, while Form 4797 separately reports the sale using the business portion’s adjusted basis.

**Maya:** What if I already filed the return for the year I sold it?

**Jordan:** Check the deadlines before filing an amendment. There may be limited relief to make the method change after filing, but amending the sale return doesn’t automatically fix a depreciation method you used for multiple years. Bring the purchase receipt, business-use records, prior returns, and sale details to a tax preparer so they can check which correction is still available.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** If I qualify for the catch-up deduction, does it increase my basis in the desk?

**Jordan:** No. The catch-up deduction and the sale are reported separately. The Section 481(a) adjustment accounts for depreciation you should have claimed. On Form 4797, you still calculate gain or loss using the freelance portion’s basis reduced by depreciation allowed or allowable. You don’t get to deduct the missed depreciation *and* use the original $360 basis to calculate the sale.

**Maya:** So I could have a deduction and taxable gain in the same year?

**Jordan:** Yes. The deduction accounts for the depreciation you missed; the gain reflects what you recovered when you sold the desk. Some or all of that gain may be ordinary income under the depreciation recapture rules.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** What would that look like with our numbers?

**Jordan:** Suppose the full $360 freelance share was allowable as depreciation in prior years, but you claimed none of it. If you qualify to catch up through Form 3115, you could have a $360 deduction from the Section 481(a) adjustment. Separately, if $120 of the sale proceeds is allocated to freelancing, you’d report $120 of ordinary income from depreciation recapture on Form 4797 because the freelance share has a $0 adjusted basis.

**Maya:** So I don’t just report a $240 loss on the sale?

**Jordan:** Right. The two amounts add up to a $240 net reduction in income in this example, but you report them separately. The sale itself produced a $120 taxable gain; the $360 deduction is for depreciation you missed in prior years.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** Does that $240 net reduction also lower my self-employment tax?

**Jordan:** Not necessarily by $240. If the desk was used in your freelance business, the $360 catch-up deduction generally reduces your Schedule C profit and can reduce your net earnings subject to self-employment tax. The $120 gain from selling the desk generally isn’t subject to self-employment tax, even though it’s ordinary income for federal income tax purposes.

**Maya:** So the two amounts don’t offset each other for self-employment tax the way they do for income tax?

**Jordan:** Right. In our example, $240 is the net reduction for income tax purposes. For self-employment tax, the starting point is the $360 reduction in Schedule C profit, not the $240 net figure.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** Does that mean I save $360 in self-employment tax?

**Jordan:** No. The $360 reduces your Schedule C profit, not your tax bill dollar for dollar. If the full 15.3% self-employment tax rate applies, the savings would be about **$51**: $360 × 92.35% × 15.3%. The $120 gain from selling the desk generally doesn’t enter that calculation.

**Maya:** Could my W-2 wages change that estimate?

**Jordan:** Yes. If your W-2 wages already reach the Social Security wage cap, the 12.4% Social Security portion won’t apply to your freelance earnings. At the regular 2.9% Medicare rate alone, the savings would be about **$10** instead.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** What if my W-2 wages are just below the Social Security cap?

**Jordan:** Then the savings could fall between $10 and $51, assuming the regular Medicare rate and enough freelance profit to absorb the full deduction. The 12.4% Social Security tax applies only to the portion of your net freelance earnings that fits under the cap after counting your W-2 Social Security wages. The 2.9% Medicare tax has no wage cap.

**Maya:** So being below the cap doesn’t automatically mean I save $51?

**Jordan:** Right. If your combined earnings are still above the cap *after* the deduction, you save about $10 in regular Medicare tax but nothing in Social Security tax. If the deduction brings your combined earnings below the cap, only the part that takes you below it saves Social Security tax.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** Can you show me what happens if the deduction takes me just below the cap?

**Jordan:** Say your W-2 Social Security wages leave $1,000 of room under the cap, and your freelance net earnings for self-employment tax are $1,200 before the deduction. The $360 deduction reduces those earnings by about $332 ($360 × 92.35%), bringing them down to about $868.

**Maya:** So only $132 of that reduction saves Social Security tax?

**Jordan:** Exactly. Before the deduction, $1,000 of your freelance earnings were subject to Social Security tax; afterward, about $868 are. You save about **$16** in Social Security tax and **$10** in regular Medicare tax, for about **$26** in total self-employment tax savings.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** Do I still get to deduct half of my self-employment tax on my income tax return?

**Jordan:** Yes. You generally deduct half of your regular self-employment tax as an adjustment to income, even if you take the standard deduction. In our example, saving about $26 in self-employment tax means that deduction is about $13 smaller.

**Maya:** So what’s the overall effect on my federal income tax calculation?

**Jordan:** The $360 catch-up deduction and the $120 gain lower your income by a net $240. The $13 reduction in your self-employment tax deduction brings the decrease in adjusted gross income to about **$227**, before any other effects. That’s a reduction in income, not a $227 reduction in your tax bill. The roughly $26 in self-employment tax savings is separate.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** If I’m in the 22% federal income tax bracket, what would I save altogether?

**Jordan:** About **$76** in this example: roughly **$50 in federal income tax** ($227 × 22%) plus **$26 in self-employment tax**. That assumes the full reduction falls in the 22% bracket and nothing else changes.

**Maya:** What else might change?

**Jordan:** If you claim the qualified business income (QBI) deduction, the catch-up expense and the ordinary depreciation recapture can affect that deduction too. So $76 is a useful estimate, but the final savings depend on the rest of your return.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** How would the QBI deduction change our $76 estimate?

**Jordan:** Suppose the $360 catch-up deduction and the $120 ordinary recapture both count toward QBI for your freelance business. Your QBI would fall by about **$227**: the $240 net reduction is partly offset by the $13 decrease in your deduction for half of self-employment tax.

**Maya:** So I’d get a smaller QBI deduction?

**Jordan:** Yes. If you’re getting the full 20% QBI deduction and no other limits apply, it would shrink by about **$45**. That leaves your taxable income about **$182 lower**, rather than $227 lower. At 22%, that’s about **$40 in federal income tax savings**, plus the same **$26 in self-employment tax savings**—about **$66 total**. The QBI deduction doesn’t change your self-employment tax.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** What if I don’t get a QBI deduction this year?

**Jordan:** If your QBI deduction is zero both with and without the desk-related amounts, there’s no QBI deduction to shrink. All else equal, the estimated savings stay at **about $76 for this year**: $50 in federal income tax and $26 in self-employment tax.

**Maya:** Could it still matter next year?

**Jordan:** Yes. If the catch-up expense creates or increases an overall QBI loss, that loss generally carries forward and offsets future QBI before you calculate the deduction. Also, even if your freelance business helps you qualify for a QBI deduction, your W-2 wages aren’t themselves QBI.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** So if my QBI deduction is zero, does that automatically mean I have a loss to carry forward?

**Jordan:** No. A zero deduction and a QBI loss are different. If your combined QBI is still positive but your taxable-income limit reduces the deduction to zero, you generally don’t carry forward that unused deduction. If your combined QBI is negative, you generally carry the loss forward to offset future QBI.

**Maya:** What would that look like with the desk?

**Jordan:** Using our estimate, the desk-related amounts reduce your QBI by about $227. If you had $100 of QBI before those amounts and no other QBI to offset the loss, you’d carry forward about **$127 in negative QBI**. That’s not a $127 deduction next year: it reduces the QBI you use to calculate next year’s deduction. If you’d otherwise qualify for the full 20% deduction and have enough QBI to absorb the loss, it would reduce that deduction by about **$25**.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** What if I only have $80 of QBI next year?

**Jordan:** The $127 carryforward would offset all $80, leaving you with no QBI deduction from that business and **$47 of negative QBI** to carry forward again, assuming you have no other QBI. The carryforward affects only the QBI deduction calculation—it doesn’t reduce your Schedule C profit or self-employment tax.

**Maya:** Do I have to keep track of it even if I can’t claim a deduction?

**Jordan:** Yes. Report and track the loss on Form 8995 or Form 8995-A, whichever applies, so you have a record of the amount available to offset future QBI.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** What if I stop freelancing before I use up that $47?

**Jordan:** Closing the freelance business generally doesn’t erase the QBI loss carryforward. If you later earn qualified business income from a new business, the $47 generally offsets that income before you calculate your QBI deduction. It can’t offset W-2 wages.

**Maya:** So if a new side business earns $200 in QBI, what happens?

**Jordan:** Assuming you have no other QBI and the full 20% rate applies, you’d subtract the $47 carryforward and calculate the deduction on $153. That’s about **$31 instead of $40**. The carryforward doesn’t reduce the new business’s Schedule C profit or self-employment tax.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** What if I go a few years without any freelance income before starting that new business?

**Jordan:** The $47 QBI loss generally carries forward through those years. Closing the old business or having a year with only W-2 wages doesn’t use it up. Keep the prior Form 8995 or 8995-A and your carryforward records so you can apply it when you next have positive QBI.

**Maya:** Can I deduct the $47 when I close the old business?

**Jordan:** No. It isn’t a separate deduction you can claim on your final Schedule C. It only reduces the qualified business income used to calculate a future QBI deduction.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** If I start that new business from home, can the $47 carryforward reduce my home-office deduction?

**Jordan:** No. The $47 carryforward applies only to the QBI calculation. It doesn’t reduce your Schedule C profit or count against the income limit for the home-office deduction. The new office still has to qualify on its own.

**Maya:** So which comes first?

**Jordan:** Figure your allowable home-office deduction on Schedule C first. That deduction generally reduces the new business’s QBI. If you have $200 of QBI *after* the home-office deduction and any other QBI adjustments, you’d then apply the $47 carryforward, leaving $153 for the QBI deduction calculation.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** What if the $200 is my QBI *before* an allowable $100 home-office deduction?

**Jordan:** Holding other QBI adjustments constant, the home-office deduction would reduce your QBI to $100. Then the $47 QBI loss carryforward would reduce it to $53. Assuming you qualify for the full 20% QBI deduction, that’s **$10.60**.

**Maya:** So both amounts reduce QBI, but only one reduces my business profit?

**Jordan:** Exactly. The $100 home-office deduction reduces your Schedule C profit and can lower your self-employment tax. The $47 carryforward only affects the QBI deduction calculation.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** What if the income limit lets me deduct only $60 of that $100 home-office expense this year?

**Jordan:** Then only the $60 you can deduct this year reduces your Schedule C profit and QBI. Holding other adjustments constant, your $200 of QBI drops to $140. After the $47 QBI loss carryforward, you have $93 left. At the full 20% rate, your QBI deduction would be **$18.60**.

**Maya:** What happens to the other $40?

**Jordan:** If you used the actual-expense method, you can generally carry the disallowed $40 forward to a later year when you use that method, subject to that year’s home-office income limit. If you used the simplified method, you can’t carry it forward. Either way, it’s separate from the $47 QBI loss carryforward, which you used up in this example.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** If I deduct that $40 next year, does it reduce next year’s QBI?

**Jordan:** Generally, yes. Under the actual-expense method, the carryover reduces your Schedule C profit and generally your QBI in the year you’re allowed to deduct it—not the year you originally paid the expense. If next year’s home-office income limit lets you deduct only $25, you’d generally carry the remaining $15 forward again.

**Maya:** Do I subtract the $47 QBI loss again next year?

**Jordan:** No. You used it up when it reduced this year’s QBI from $140 to $93. The only amount still carrying forward in this example is the unused home-office expense.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** What if I switch to the simplified method next year?

**Jordan:** You can use the simplified method if your home office still qualifies, but you can’t deduct the $40 actual-expense carryover that year. It isn’t lost: you can generally use it in a later year when you return to the actual-expense method, subject to that year’s home-office income limit.

**Maya:** What reduces my QBI in the simplified-method year, then?

**Jordan:** Only the home-office deduction you’re allowed to claim that year under the simplified method. The $40 stays on hold, and the $47 QBI loss doesn’t come back—you already used it up.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** Can you show me what that looks like with numbers?

**Jordan:** Say you have $200 of QBI before the home-office deduction and can claim $75 under the simplified method. Holding other adjustments constant, that leaves $125 of QBI. If you qualify for the full 20% deduction, your QBI deduction is **$25**. You don’t subtract the $40 actual-expense carryover or the $47 QBI loss you already used.

**Maya:** What if I switch back to actual expenses the following year?

**Jordan:** Then you can generally deduct the $40 carryover to the extent that year’s home-office income limit allows. If you can use only $15, that $15 generally reduces that year’s Schedule C profit and QBI, and the remaining $25 carries forward.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** Can I use that $15 carryover on top of my current-year home-office expenses?

**Jordan:** Only if there’s room under that year’s home-office income limit. If the Form 8829 calculation leaves $15 available for the carryover, you deduct $15 and carry the remaining $25 forward. If there’s no room, the full $40 generally stays on hold.

**Maya:** Where do I find the $40 if last year’s return used the simplified method?

**Jordan:** Look back to Form 8829 from the last year you used actual expenses. Keep that form with your records: the carryover doesn’t get deducted in the simplified-method year, so you’ll need the earlier figures when you switch back.

speaker: A
text:
**Maya:** Do I enter the whole $40 on Form 8829, or just the $15 I can deduct?

**Jordan:** Enter the full $40 in the applicable carryover category. Form 8829 applies this year’s limit and calculates both the amount you can deduct and the amount that carries forward. So in our example, $15 goes into this year’s home-office deduction, and $25 remains for a future year.

**Maya:** What if the old form splits the $40 between operating expenses and depreciation?

**Jordan:** Keep those amounts separate when you bring them forward. Form 8829 applies the income limit in stages, with operating expenses generally coming before depreciation. Use the carryover breakdown from the last Form 8829 you filed, even if you used the simplified method in the intervening year.

speaker: B
text:
**Maya:** What if the $40 is split into $10 of operating expenses and $30 of depreciation, and there’s room for only $15 after this year’s expenses?

**Jordan:** Assuming this year’s expenses leave $15 available for those carryovers, you’d generally deduct the **$10 operating-expense carryover first**, then **$5 of the depreciation carryover**. The remaining **$25 carries forward in the depreciation category**. Enter the full $10 and $30 in their respective categories on Form 8829 and let the form apply the limits.
